params.title: Other Equipment and Networks
params.subtitle: Computers, Ethernet, NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000, depth finders, gyro compasses, SSAS, AIS, electronic charts, auto pilots and data recorders.

onScreen: Computers, networks, NMEA, navigation equipment and data recorders
scenes.narration: This lesson covers the other electronics you will maintain aboard ship. We'll start with troubleshooting computers and Ethernet networks. Then come the 2 marine data networks from the National Marine Electronics Association, or NMEA: NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000. After that: depth finders, gyro compasses, the Ship Security Alert System and the Automatic Identification System. We finish with electronic charts, auto pilots and the Vessel Data Recorder. First up, computers.

params.title: Printer won't print, or no display?
items: Printer won't print: frozen printer queue, out of toner or ink, or a paper jam
Not a likely reason: a defective graphics card, which only drives the monitor
No display: bad video card, bad 15 pin video connector, or no power to the monitor
Not the cause: a CD-ROM drive or a fragmented hard drive

onScreen: Printer: frozen queue, no toner or ink, paper jam
No display: video card, 15 pin video connector, monitor power
Not a CD-ROM drive or a fragmented hard drive
scenes.narration: 2 quick troubleshooting questions. First, a printer won't print a document. Likely reasons are a frozen printer queue, a printer out of toner or ink, or a paper jam. A defective graphics card is not a likely reason, because the graphics card only drives the monitor. Second, there's no display on the monitor. The most likely causes are a bad video card, a bad 15 pin video connector, or no power to the monitor. A CD-ROM drive or a fragmented hard drive has nothing to do with it.

blocks.label: Bootstrap loader
blocks.note: Finds and starts the operating system

blocks.label: Operating system
blocks.note: Loads printer drivers, not the BIOS

blocks.label: BIOS setup
blocks.note: Won't boot? Check the BIOS settings

onScreen: Bootstrap loader starts the operating system
Printer drivers: loaded by the operating system
BIOS setup: check settings if it won't boot
scenes.narration: The BIOS, the basic input-output system, has 4 main functions. When the power comes on, it runs P.O.S.T., the power-on self-test. Next, the bootstrap loader finds and starts the operating system. Printer drivers are not a BIOS function; the operating system loads those. The other 2 functions are BIOS setup and the BIOS drivers. If the power is on but the computer will not boot into the operating system, use the BIOS setup mode to check for proper BIOS settings, such as the boot device order and drive detection.

params.title: Windows XP drives: find them, replace them

blocks.label: System Information
blocks.note: Shows the type of disc drives

blocks.label: Replacement drive
blocks.note: Speed and transfer rate need not match

onScreen: System Information shows the disc drive types
Replacement CD-ROM drive: same interface as the old one
Speed and data transfer rate need not match
scenes.narration: To determine the type of disc drives in a Windows XP system, click Start, then Programs, then Accessories, and then System Information. Now suppose you are replacing a CD-ROM drive. The old drive uses an interface system such as IDE/ATAPI, SATA or SCSI. The important consideration is that the replacement drive should use the same interface system as the old drive. Its speed and data transfer rate don't have to match.

params.title: Ethernet: a star around the central hub

onScreen: Each node: a home-run cable back to the central hub
Same collision domain: bandwidth shared between all nodes
scenes.narration: Now Ethernet. Ethernet nodes are interconnected in a star. Each node, whether it's a computer or a printer, has its own cable making a home run back to the central hub. All of these nodes are in the same collision domain. Within the same collision domain, the available bandwidth is shared between all the nodes, because only 1 of them can transmit at a time.

params.title: Ethernet and USB cables
rows: Not what these systems generally use
5 meters max: hub to hub or hub to peripheral

onScreen: USB 2.0: 5 meters max between hubs or hub and peripheral
scenes.narration: Now the cables. 10Base-T and 100Base-TX systems generally use CAT-5 cable with 4 twisted pairs. Not coax, and not fiber optic. Next, USB, the Universal Serial Bus. The maximum length of a USB 2.0 cable between 2 hubs, or between a hub and a peripheral, is 5 meters.

params.title: Setting up a router
items: Open a web browser
Enter the router's address for network admin
Enter the username and password: no internet download needed
For the exam, common router addresses: 192.168.1.1, 192.168.0.1 and 192.168.2.0
In practice, 192.168.2.0 is normally a network address; the usual default is 192.168.2.1

scenes.narration: Installing a router? The initial steps are simple. Open a web browser, enter the router's address for network admin, and then enter the username and password. No internet download is needed. For the exam, the most commonly used router IP, or Internet Protocol, addresses are 192.168.1.1, 192.168.0.1 and 192.168.2.0. In practice, 192.168.2.0 is normally a network address, and the usual default is 192.168.2.1. But on the exam, choose the set with 192.168.1.1, 192.168.0.1 and 192.168.2.0.

blocks.label: Talker
blocks.note: Shield grounded to this chassis only

onScreen: Serial data, 1 bit at a time
Shield grounded to the talker chassis only
scenes.narration: NMEA 0183 uses serial data communication. It sends its sentences 1 bit at a time. It is not parallel, not Ethernet, and not a Controller Area Network, or CAN, bus. Only 1 talker is allowed on each line, and it sends to several listeners. In an NMEA 0183 system, opto-isolators must be used, and the cable shield should be grounded to the talker chassis only. Grounding the shield at that 1 end prevents ground loops.

onScreen: NMEA 0183 data: HyperTerminal on a PC
scenes.narration: Here's an important difference between NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000: single talker versus multi-talkers. NMEA 0183 is serial and allows only 1 talker per line. NMEA 2000 is a CAN bus with multiple talkers on the same network. For logging and troubleshooting NMEA 0183 data, a typical PC program used widely is HyperTerminal. NMEA 2000 data needs a gateway, which we'll come to shortly.

params.title: NMEA 0183: electrical facts
items: Current and most recent version: the RS422 standard for data communications
A unit must handle a maximum signal voltage range of ±15 volts without damage
Opto-isolators must be used
Shield grounded to the talker chassis only: no ground loops

onScreen: Shield grounded at the talker chassis only
scenes.narration: 2 more NMEA 0183 facts. The current and most recent version of NMEA 0183 uses the RS422 standard for data communications. And an NMEA 0183 unit must be capable of handling a maximum signal voltage range of plus or minus 15 volts without damage. Keep the wiring rule with them: opto-isolators must be used, and the shield is grounded to the talker chassis only, which prevents ground loops.

onScreen: Drop cable to a device: 6 meters max
Gateway translates messages for a PC
scenes.narration: NMEA 2000 networks are built from backbone cables, tees, drop cables, power cables and terminating resistors. The backbone runs from a terminating resistor at one end, through the tees, to a terminating resistor at the other end. Each device connects to a tee with a drop cable, and the maximum length for a drop cable to a single NMEA 2000 device is 6 meters. A power cable feeds the backbone. Multiplexers, combiners and routers are not NMEA 2000 components. And because NMEA 2000 is a CAN bus, viewing its data requires a gateway, which translates its messages for the viewing equipment, such as a PC.

params.title: Load Equivalency Numbers (LENs)
params.answer: A 3 LEN device draws up to 150 mA

scenes.narration: NMEA 2000 certified devices state their current requirements in LENs, which stands for Load Equivalency Numbers. 1 LEN is equal to 50 milliamps. So a device rated at 3 LEN draws up to 3 times 50 milliamps, or 150 milliamps. That's the number to hold on to: 1 LEN equals 50 milliamps.

params.title: NMEA 2000 numbers to remember
items: Backbone power supply pair: maintained within 9 to 16 volts
1 LEN = 50 mA
For the exam, backbone operating speed: 250 bps (the real rate is 250 kbit/s)
Drop cable to a single device: 6 meters max
Viewing the data requires a gateway

scenes.narration: Let's collect the NMEA 2000 numbers. The voltage of the backbone power supply pair must be maintained within 9 to 16 volts. 1 LEN equals 50 milliamps. For the exam, the backbone operating speed is keyed as 250 bits per second. The real backbone runs at 250 kilobits per second, but choose 250 bits per second on the exam. A drop cable to a single device can be at most 6 meters long. And to view NMEA 2000 data, you need a gateway.

params.title: Depth finder pulses
labels: Short pulses: fine resolution in shallow water

scenes.narration: Now depth finders. Depth finding equipment commonly uses frequencies of 200 to 400 kilohertz. It transmits in pulses, and common pulse widths are 25 to 600 microseconds. Short pulses give fine resolution in shallow water. Longer pulses are used for deeper soundings. So remember the pair: 200 to 400 kilohertz, and 25 to 600 microseconds.

params.title: Gyro compasses
rows: Voltage regulation, as a variable resistor
3 coils and a dual-axis electronic level sensor
Finds true north, with no spinning rotor

onScreen: Older gyro: carbon pile gives voltage regulation
Fiber-optic gyro: 3 fiber-optic coils and a dual-axis electronic level sensor
scenes.narration: Next, gyro compasses. On an older gyro compass, the carbon pile provides voltage regulation. It works as a variable resistor. A fiber-optic gyro compass has no spinning rotor at all. It uses 3 fiber-optic coils and a dual-axis electronic level sensor to determine the direction of true north.

onScreen: No all ships alert on VHF-DSC or MF-HF
scenes.narration: The Ship Security Alert System, or SSAS, operates by sending a covert alert through the ship's Inmarsat-C terminal to specific addresses. It does not send an all ships alert. Not on VHF, or very high frequency, digital selective calling, known as DSC, and not on MF-HF, the medium and high frequency bands. Because the alert is covert, it goes only to those specific addresses, not to the ships around you.

AIS, the Automatic Identification System, uses 2 VHF channels. Channel 87B is 161.975 megahertz, and channel 88B is 162.025 megahertz. AIS units send their data at 9.6 kbs, that's kilobits per second, using GMSK modulation, which stands for Gaussian minimum shift keying. So: 87B and 88B, 161.975 and 162.025 megahertz, and 9.6 kbs GMSK.

params.title: Electronic chart systems
items: C-Map charts: enter license information for each computer being used
Not just once in a master terminal
Data inputs include position, speed, depth and radar
SSAS is not a chart input: "Radar, SSAS and Position" is incorrect

onScreen: C-Map: license information on each computer
scenes.narration: Electronic chart systems include ECDIS, the Electronic Chart Display and Information System. Before using C-Map charts for an electronic chart system, license information must be entered for each computer being used, not just in a master terminal. The system's data inputs include position, speed, depth and radar. SSAS is not a chart input, so the list radar, SSAS and position is the incorrect one.

onScreen: Auto pilot drives the steering gear
Rudder feedback unit: necessary, reports rudder angle
scenes.narration: The inputs normally required for an auto pilot are course information and rudder feedback. The auto pilot takes the course information and orders the steering gear to move the rudder. GPS, the Global Positioning System, can be a useful extra input, but it is not necessary. The necessary component is the rudder feedback unit. It reports the actual rudder angle back to the auto pilot, closing the loop.

params.title: Vessel Data Recorder (VDR) inputs
rows: Date, time, position, speed and heading
Depth of water, radar, audio from the bridge

onScreen: Recorded: date, time, position, speed, heading
Depth of water, radar, bridge audio, VHF radio, rudder feedback
scenes.narration: The Vessel Data Recorder, or VDR, records items such as the date, time, position, speed and heading, the depth of water, radar, audio from the bridge, and VHF radio communications. Rudder feedback may be an input too. But 2 things are not VDR inputs: EGC data, from Enhanced Group Call, and MSI, which is Maritime Safety Information. So any list that includes EGC data or MSI is the wrong one.

params.title: How long the VDR keeps its data

badges.label: Data Acquisition Unit (DAU)
badges.note: May have data storage this long

onScreen: Crash Survivable Module: up to 12 hours
Data Acquisition Unit: as long as 30 days
scenes.narration: 2 parts of the Vessel Data Recorder to know. The Crash Survivable Module, or CSM, retains data for up to 12 hours. The Data Acquisition Unit, or DAU, may have data storage for as long as 30 days. So: up to 12 hours in the crash survivable module, and as long as 30 days in the data acquisition unit.
